Sponsor: Antec C8 with fans on Newegg https://howl.me/cmXtq5tnNJ7 - and without fans on Newegg https://howl.me/cmXtsXoSlzL
The Intel Arc B570 Battlemage graphics card is in for review today. Our benchmarks of the B570 GPU include testing on low-end CPUs, like the i5-12400 and R5 5600X, and on an unbound AMD 9800X3D Ryzen CPU. Benchmarking looks at gaming performance and driver overhead of the top video cards in 2025 -- for now -- as we prepare for the NVIDIA RTX 50 series launch. NVIDIA's RTX 5090, 5080, 5070 Ti, and 5070 are around the corner. In theory, AMD's RX 9070 series also loom. Until then, we have Intel's Arc B570 video card to test, bringing in a card in the $220 to $230 price point to freshen up the low-end. Our benchmarking considers gaming performance, efficiency and power consumption, and scaling across multiple CPUs for our standardized test suite.

Find our prior Intel B580 review here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JjdCkSsLYLk

comments.text: I really wish they would have took the techpowerup approach and included the 4060 Ti 8gb and 16gb versions. Their benchmarks were interesting in two ways; first it showed that Intel is making progress on their GPUs (good for competition). Secondly, it would have shown the difference between 8gb and 16gb of vram on a 4060 Ti. Contrary to popular belief, the difference was non-existent in most games. In a small handful number of games, you'd get a few extra FPS, literally, just a few. Heck, in Cyberpunk in 4k, the 8gb actually beat the 16gb. Obviously that was margin of error but still. It goes to show that people are severely overvaluing and overestimating vram on low & mid-tier cards like the 4060 Ti. Just to be clear, the difference is way higher on higher end GPUs that have the horsepower, bandwidth and bus width to utilize all that ram.

comments.text:
With Gamers Nexus having tested 7 games & Hardware Unboxed having tested 50 games (with a 5600/X), I'm strongly leaning towards Hardware Unboxed's findings in terms of consumer value.

Even Hardware Unboxed's initial 12 game review, which saw the B580 8.4% faster than the RTX 4060 (using a 9800X3D), found it to be 1% slower (in 50 games) with a R5 5600.... That's a pretty massive swing...Meaningful, even before you get into the troubling FPS lows everyone has found. As a consumer, this information is useful to me.

Hardware Unboxed's 13 game review video today using real scenarios consumers would use today, namely testing both Native & 1440p/Quality upscaling & 9800X3D Vs R5 5600, netted similar results. At frame-rates that matter...

No one's buying a $650 9800X3D to use with a $250 B580 at the end of the day. Nor would they be willing to wait for a 9800X3D class CPU to become available at a price point that makes sense to pair with a B580. This is the most realistic consumer scenario we have. Why would they, if they could just keep their 12400/5600 and get a $550 RTX 5070? Which will be more than 100% more powerful in raster alone...

With the new GPU's from AMD/Nvidia releasing soon, none of this really matters anyway. Intel isn't competing with two year old graphics cards. I'm happy they are making progress but dissapointed that they are only competing with themselves in that regard....

comments.text:
@nimbydimby
 Let’s break this down because you’re clearly trying to sound smarter than you actually are. First off, the “Intel GPUs have issues with CPU overhead” is such a hot take, it’s practically on fire with the obvious. Thanks for pointing out the blindingly obvious thing that everybody already knows, Sherlock. But then, you continue on to act like your “knowledge” is some deep dive into GPU performance. If you really think pointing out that Intel has CPU overhead issues somehow makes you a tech guru, you're sadly mistaken.

You bring up GN and claim their game suite is "limited"—six games? Is that the best you can do to discredit them? You know there are hundreds of game benchmarks out there, right? Just because you don’t agree with their testing methods doesn’t mean they’re useless. You sound like a keyboard warrior trying to invalidate someone else’s work because it doesn't fit into your little box.

And here’s where you start digging deeper into stupidity: “Take a look at HW Unboxed”? Oh wow, you just linked a video like it’s some magical piece of proof that can override any counterargument. Nice try, but no one’s impressed by you playing the “here’s a YouTuber’s opinion” card. Your whole argument boils down to two games, ARMA and War Thunder, like those are somehow the pinnacle of “CPU intensive” benchmarking? What do you expect them to do—run every game under the sun just to please your whining? You’re acting like there’s some grand conspiracy because you didn’t get the results you wanted from a handful of titles.

And the cherry on top is this masterstroke: "With mid to lower end CPUs, Nvidia and AMD perform better in CPU intensive games." You don’t say? I had no idea, thanks for the earth-shattering revelation. It’s almost like different hardware performs differently based on the type of workload. If this was groundbreaking news, I'd be giving you a standing ovation. Instead, you just proved that not only do you lack a full understanding of benchmarks, but you're also out here recycling basic observations like they’re Pulitzer-worthy.

Next time you try to sound intelligent, at least throw out something new or helpful instead of playing the “here’s a random YouTube video that supports my point” game. Keep it up, though. You're really making a strong case for why we shouldn't listen to you at all.

comments.text:
I remember someone with more information than most mentioning long before the introduction of the first B580 cards that the Battlemage architecture was a bit disappointing and that Intel planned to forgo the enthusiast cards for the B generation. The same person said that Celestial on the other hand looked like it would be better than they had projected, and that it was close to being ready for production so that's where the next enthusiast cards would be. Now that was a few months before the B580 got released, and I have no idea if these statements are true, but I can't help but hope they are. Then the real question is just how far the development of Celestial has proceeded, and how long it will take before Intel feel it's a good idea to leapfrog to the next gen.

A long time ago, before the Alchemist was even taped out, I posted a prediction based on what I know of the history of graphics controllers developed by Intel. I predicted that Alchemist would be pretty much a fail as even if the hardware was decent the drivers would be crap. And at first I was very right. The drivers were a total failure while the hardware was at least pretty decent. I continued my prediction with saying Battelmage would be a improvement on the hardware and a real attempt at improving the drivers. Then I predicted that Celestial would be able to match up with the low to mid range cards from Nvidia nad AMD, but the drivers, while a lot better than for Alchemist, was still not up to scratch. Druid is where I though Intel would be able to start competing with Nvidia and AMD both with the hardware and the software stack.

Now the logic was based on the past graphics drivers from Intel and just how advanced the GPU hardware has become. Last time before Alchemist that Intel was doing discrete graphics was the i740 back in 98 I think. That's over 20 year ago, and the games and drivers has changes a lot since then.
My concerns about the drivers were largely proven correct as Intel had decided that DirectX 12 were where they would put their time and money. Meanwhile they only had very basic  support for DX9 to DX11, and those are still often used by decently modern games. But the Alchemist drivers really didn't work well with those.

But Intel really surprised me as they "borrowed" code from Linux, Wine I think, to support the older DX versions, and it was a big improvement. Not perfect, but it was huge as a stopgap.

Now what has been a downer is the fact that Intel has stumbled into huge financial trouble. At one time it looked as if they were about to cancel the ARC project and we either only would get a Battlemage release as a last gasp, or perhaps not even that. But later there were indication that they were still going to do both Battlemage and Celestial, possibly even Druid. I really hope they are able to get that far and that the GPU has started to make money so Intel can continue the development. This would be good for the market as it's pretty silly that we only have two real alternatives for all the computers all over the world. And no I'm not counting the current crop of processors with integrated GPU. The new AMD something Ai something looks promising with it's really wide memory bus, but it's still not really enough to compete with discrete graphics cards. ARM is supposedly working on a GPU, but exactly what that will mean is not really known right now. But three brands is 50% more than two brands. Lets just hope that AMD and Intel is able to compete with Nvidia over time.

comments.text: @rattlehead999  I get where you're coming from now! The confusion is understandable. The 7 series and 9 series are on a 28 nm process node.  10 series = 16 nm. 20 series = 12 nm. 30 series = 8 nm. A direct area comparison doesn't tell us a thing. comments.author: @auturgicflosculator2183

comments.text:
@auturgicflosculator2183  
Die size comparison is not based on the node itself, it's based on the reticle limit.

TSMC 28nm has a reticle limit of 640mm^2
TSMC 12/16nm has a reticle limit of 841mm^2
Samsung 8nm, TSMC 7nm and 5nm have a reticle limit of 851-858mm^2

A mid-range chip is a chip that is roughly half the reticle limit of the process node.

80 class cards were usually 80-90% the reticle limit and 60 class cards were roughly half of the 80 class cards.

This goes for any Integrated Circuit(IC) chip, not just GPUs, be it CPU, FPGA, ASIC, micro controller, etc, etc.
comments.author: @rattlehead999

comments.text:
@rattlehead999  If reticle limit directly dictated GPU class, GP102's 471 mm² out of a maximum reticle limit of 841² would be considered a mid-sized die, not a high-end chip.

Your logic is not making any sense for the 10-series. The math is way off. It makes perfect sense though, for the 40-series and beyond.
comments.author: @auturgicflosculator2183

comments.text:
@auturgicflosculator2183  You don't adjust for process node size... you adjust it to Reticle Limit.

No, the Reticle Limit is dictated by the technology used to produce the process node. 

Process nodes produced using Near-Ultraviolet Lithography(28nm) had a reticle limit of 640mm^2
DUV used in 16/12nm and first gen 7nm has a reticle limit of 851mm^2
EUV used in second gen 7nm and later have a reticle limit of 858mm^2.

You never want to be 100% reticle limit, you want to never go beyond 90%, so 90% is the new 100% and half of that is mid-range. 

The cost comes from the wafers and R&D and die size determines cost, performance is a byproduct
comments.author: @rattlehead999

comments.text:
@rattlehead999  GP104 was the more efficient die, with better early yields. The 1080 chip was a bit smaller in surface area than previous 80 class cards, adjusted for process size, but larger than previous 70 class cards. That said, it was more efficient and had fewer defects. The 1080 Ti was the only remotely consumer-class GPU to use the GP102 die. That was more for the Titans and Quadros.

The real shift may have started with the 30 series. It had die areas larger than the previous gen, which may have set expectations even higher...the 3070 was closer to a 2080 die size than to historical 70 class cards. Then the 4070 was closer to 60 class than to historical 70 class cards, further confusing matters with an apparent over-correction, and the 50-series following suit.

Again you do NOT multiply the die size by the amount shrank by the process node...

GP102 was a slightly above mid-range chip.

Companies pay for die size, NOT for performance. 

And in the past Gx100 was the 80 class card. Then it became the Gx102 and finally with Pascal the Gx104(GP104) was the 80 class card, even the freaking code name of the chip was from the previous generations' 60 class cards...
The gtx 280, 480 and 580 were all GT/GF100
The gtx 680 was the first scam where it was literally even called a 660 in slides to investors and 3 weeks later renamed gtx 680 when it launched.
The gtx 780 was a GK110, which signified 2nd gen Kepler with the second digit, effectively a Gx100 chip too.
